why: It is the Chinese state's own post below the county seat, which a town map might otherwise be tempted to draw at a town gate. Its two footnotes (the Wenxian tongkao and Gu Yanwu's Rizhilu) support only its opening sentence, and it lists two modern works as sources. Its figure of forty-two posts set up in Fujian in 1387 carries no citation, and the Mingshi's biography of Zhou Dexing (juan 132) gives forty-five, so the number is not to be taken from here. Its ninth rank is stated by the Qing example. It says the posts answered to local officials but that the Ministry of War controlled their setting up, closing and evaluation. The office changed by dynasty: under the Yuan it was non-permanent and military, and it multiplied in the late Qing. It says nothing of where a post stood or what it looked like.

It describes the walled Chinese market as a built thing: each Han market a square with its own walls and gates, a market tower at the center from which officials oversaw it, and storehouses behind the shops against the market wall; the Tang capital's two markets each took two wards. It describes the capital only, ; it says nothing of a county town's market. Its Han market (each a square of 266 bu, with a five-story tower) follows later literary texts rather than excavation, and its own figures disagree: it gives the Han East and West markets unequal areas, and the Tang East Market an east-west width of 24 meters beside an area of 0.92 square kilometres. It is used for the shape of a market, not for any of its measurements.

It says what a ward's machi-kaisho was for - the ward officials posted there passed on the magistrate's notices and drew up the residents' papers - and that cities differed: Osaka had one in every ward, while in Edo the ward headman's residence served as the kaisho. The passage on what the ward officials did there cites nothing, and the Osaka detail rests on a single 1997 local-history newsletter, so it can show what the practice looked like but not supply a figure. It describes the great cities of the Edo period, not a place of our size, and in Edo the name 町会所 also meant the one city-wide relief-fund office set up after the Kansei reforms, which was not a ward's office. It says nothing of the building's size or where on the street it stood.

It dates the institution (the earliest known, in Beijing, from the Yongle reign of the early fifteenth century) and says what it began as and became - a place of fellowship and lodging for people from one home region, then for some a merchants' association. Its one scholarly citation (Qiu Pengsheng's 1989 study of eighteenth- and nineteenth-century Suzhou trade associations) is attached to its definition, not to the Yongle date, which it gives without a source; the date is the stub's claim, which a scholarly history of the huiguan (He Bingdi's of 1966, for one) would have to carry. It says nothing of county towns, of the building, or of where it stood.

It describes the Chinese collection as a trade: night-soil men collecting daily from households and dry latrines, some cleaning chamber pots, each belonging to a night-soil yard with its own fixed routes. It describes the capital from the late Qing into the Republican years; it says nothing of a county town or of earlier centuries.

It shows that a masugata gate stood on the outer works of the shogun's own castle, not only at its core. It is a short tertiary article with no references at all (the page carries Wikipedia's banner for an unsourced article). It gives the 36 mitsuke as a traditional figure ("there are said to have been 36"), not a count of gates, so the number sets the scale and is not an exact tally. It is about Edo, the largest castle in Japan, so it says nothing about the gates of a provincial castle town.

It corroborates the yamen's area from a second readable page. The page is a tour operator's promotional copy with no source for its dimensions, and it describes the restored museum; two weak pages agreeing is not verification.

It describes the canal city that the record's river cities draw their in-city canals from, and states the bank form - stone revetment, railings in places, stepped house landings - in plain words. It describes the city's canals from the plan and from what survives without dating the revetments or measuring anything; it is used for the bank form and for how the moat met the city's canals, never for a number. Suzhou is also a particular case: a prefectural seat of nearly 300,000 people (the article's 1184 count) in the canal country of the lower Yangzi, among the richest cities of the empire, so stone-faced banks along its canals show what a large, wealthy canal city built, not what a smaller or poorer river city, or one outside that region, would have lined its banks with. It posts under an account named for astrology, with no named author, so it is corroborated where it can be (the paired land-and-water gates by pingjiang-tu, the moat-canal junction at Pan Gate by pan-gate-enwiki).

It attests that a real aqueduct carried a purpose-built spillway, which is why our capital's aqueduct is drawn with one. Its limit is that its case discharged to a valley rather than a moat. The page gives no date for the spillway itself, so its Edo-period existence rests on the page's framing rather than on a dated statement.

It places a real Edo-period city's produce market on its riverbank, along the Okawa, and names it one of Osaka's three great markets with the Dojima rice market and the Zakoba fish market; it does not put the fish market beside it (Zakoba stood on the Hyakkenbori canal in the west of the city). It is a short article with no references of its own, mostly on the market's privileges and quarrels; it says nothing of its buildings, and of why it moved to the river it says only that its previous site was inconvenient. It was the licensed monopoly market of one of Japan's three great cities, so its riverbank site speaks for a large river city, not a town.

It is standard reference work on the one granary our capital's stipend granary and brokers' row are modeled on, and it states plainly both its waterside siting and the merchant street in front of it. Its limits are that this was the shogunate's central granary for Edo, many times the size of anything a domain seat built, so its form transfers and its scale does not.

It establishes the overlord's reserve rice as a thing kept INSIDE castles and bound to them, which is the contrast that explains why a working granary stood elsewhere, and it names the castle's own arms as the same kind of castle-bound holding. It describes the shogunate's system of stocking its vassals' castles, an arrangement between overlord and vassal that the setting's own notes do not describe for the Emperor. Even in Japan, "inside the castle" is the narrow sense only: part of the stock sat at the Tōkaidō post stations, and in the broad sense 城米 means all the tax rice of the shogunate's own lands. The castle-bound war reserve is also the seventeenth-century arrangement; from 1689 some was sold for the shogunate's finances, and later it went to famine relief and price control.

It gives the ringed moats of the imperial capital and where their water came from and went, the Chinese anchor for our capital's engineered moat ring. Beijing was the imperial capital, so its moat ring is a ceiling and not a norm, and the dimensions mix the period specification with a 1953 survey of a much-altered work.

It sets out what a period map of a castle and its town was required to show - the works, the keep and turrets, every street - which is the precedent for our castle drawn as works without rooms. The standards are one domain's record of the order, and the page lists what the plans had to show and says their written notes were in principle confined to militarily important matters (citing Senda 2001), but it says nothing of what the drawings left out, so that they drew no residences is our reading; the plans themselves, viewable in the National Archives of Japan digital archive, would show it directly.

We use it for one fact: until the Second World War many graves were built on a corner of a household's own land or kept by a neighborhood group, so a burial place beside the settlement, not a central one, was ordinary. Its limits are that it gives no source for the sentence, no period earlier than the twentieth century and no share of households, and does not say how far from the houses such graves lay.

We use it for one fact: under the Edo temple registration, making one's grave at one's parish temple was half an obligation - the one pull toward a grave away from the household's own settlement. Its limits are that the sentence gives no date of its own (the Edo period comes from the surrounding passage); it does not say whether the grave meant the body's or the visited one; and it says nothing of how far the parish temple lay.

We use it for where each grave of the two lay: the grave where the body lay, most often on common land and set on a riverbank, a hillside or a beach away from the houses, marked with no more than a stone and reused in order of death, and the visited grave in the precinct of a temple or hall in the village (in one entry, within the house plot); and for its distribution. Its limits are that the entries disagree on the northeast (one has the custom reaching Tōhoku, another hardly seen there) and agree only that Kyūshū hardly has it; that none gives a distance from the houses or says how many a village kept - they say only that the burial grave lay away from the houses (Mypedia), beyond the village boundary on one theory (Yamakawa), or anywhere from far outside the village to beside the visited grave (Britannica); and that the custom is the one twentieth-century folklorists recorded, which the Heibonsha entry dates to the early Edo period at the earliest and Nipponica says in some places arose only when cemeteries were reorganized after Meiji.

It gives the count of eta, hinin and monkey-trainers' households under the Kanto head in a return of about 1800, which is the scale of a whole region's outcaste population, not of one town's quarter. The encyclopedias on the page differ in small things - one dates the count to 1800 and counts the hinin in households, another to the Kansei era and counts them in huts - and it describes Edo, the Kanto and the parts of Izu, Kai, Suruga and Mutsu under the same head only. The count is the head's own return to the shogunate (a kakiage, as the Nipponica entry calls it), repeated secondhand, and it takes in the households under him directly and indirectly, so it is the figure a head gave for his whole jurisdiction, not a census of the settlements in it.

It is the one page read that gives a count of gates below the great cities - one to several blocks, against one to each block in a large town - and it describes the gate's form. Dictionary and encyclopedia entries that give no references of their own, all of them on Japan. The entries place the gates chiefly in the great cities - Edo, Kyoto, Osaka - and the form, the closing hour and the keeper's night round they give are the city of Edo's. The count is one sentence of the old Sekai Daihyakka's entry on the gate, written of the great cities and not of any named town. Its 町 can be read as a ward-block rather than a town (a large block with a gate of its own, small blocks sharing one), so it gives a shape for a small town, not a figure. The Nipponica entry is by Inagaki Fumio, a period-drama consultant and novelist rather than a historian, and the entries give the great gate's width in two slightly different figures.

It gives Edo's count of samurai-quarter guard boxes, a box's size and staff, and the one provincial case read, Aizu-Wakamatsu, whose town-run boxes made night rounds. Its count (936 samurai-run boxes, in the Genbun years, 1736-41) is Edo's, a city of about a million, and leaves out the shogunate's boxes and the town-run jishinban. The box size and the four or five staff are a "usual" figure from one entry, by the period-drama consultant Inagaki Shisei, and Heibonsha has the staff set instead by each lord's stipend. The Aizu staffing is hedged ("it seems"), and it counts no provincial town's boxes.

It is the one page read that sizes a samurai archery ground and says where it stood. Its figures are the standard it says warrior houses set, not a survey of real ranges, and they are Japanese only: no Chinese archery ground is sized here. A breadth of one bow-length is at most a single shooting lane; the entry does not size the shooting hall or the ground around it. The entry is short and names no town. The page's second sense is the Edo paid archery parlour: from about 1789 it shot at 7.5 ken (about 13.5 m) in temple precincts and amusement quarters, and it was a front for unlicensed prostitution. That parlour is another institution, and none of its figures or places size the samurai ground.

It gives the temple's name, its origin and its position beside the quarter it served, the case this page uses for a burial ground standing near the wall. The distance is our own measurement. The page attests the temple's nearness to the pleasure quarter, not to any wall - Edo had none, so the wall is our frame - and the throw-in burials are one disaster episode of 1855 at the end of the period, not a standing practice.

It says the domains built practice structures for the contest and names five that had a dogata, a wooden mock-up of the hall that was sometimes full length and sometimes only the top of the arrow's arc, which shows archery practice as a built place a domain kept. It hedges the list as hearsay and the sentence carries no citation. It gives the practice and not a count or a size. It does not say the structures stood in the castle town; its one located example, Sendai's, was on ground bounded by the Hirose river so stray arrows fell in the water. The contest was a 17th-century Japanese specialty of the great domains. The article's own bibliography names a closer study, Irie Kohei's 2007 paper on the dosha facilities in Budogaku Kenkyu 40(2), which this record did not read.

It places a provincial capital's drill ground at a gate and gives its size, and its gazetteer footnote says barracks were built at its sides. Of its size figures only the Ming gazetteer's "broad four li" is carried by a reference, while the four-li round (given in the modern li of 500 m) and the "over thirty mu" are uncited, and the two do not agree (a four-li round is far more than thirty mu). The barracks line is only in the footnote, and those barracks were raised in the early Wanli years to house troops brought in from elsewhere against the wokou raids, an emergency measure rather than a standing arrangement; and it is one provincial capital.

It measures one garrison quarter against its city: about 2.05 by 1.55 km, some 3 square km, a little over a quarter of the walled city. That is a modern measurement from the Xi'an city gazetteer (西安市志); the only Qing measure it gives is 1,028 by 1,200 paces. It says the drill ground lay inside the quarter, on the old Ming palace site, and was used on fixed days each month (it does not say how many). The quarter was the Qing conquest dynasty's banner garrison, walled off from the townspeople, and it stands in here for garrison quarters in general. Its share changed: from 1683 to about 1780 a southern annex gave the garrison nearly the whole east of the city. It is not an upper bound, since Jingzhou's banner quarter took the eastern half of its city and drilled outside the south gate.

It gives the magazine's place outside the city on a highway, its ground and its guard. Its account of the guard does not match the Suginami ward's site-marker text: the column has the magazine's officials guarding it day and night, while the marker says three officials lived there in yearly turns and the guarding was a labour levy on 16 nearby villages. It never says why the magazine stood outside the city; it ties the site to the highway's military role, so "outside the city" is our reading of its location. And the magazine was the shogunate's in Edo, not a domain's.

It names what stood inside a samurai house's gate - a roofed well and a rice storehouse - in a surviving house. It describes one house as preserved today (its grounds now run as a museum, so the layout a visitor sees may not be exactly the Edo one), and Kakunodate was a small northern castle town whose samurai served a branch of the Satake house.

It attests that a working towpath is carried over the channels that interrupt it, which is how our towpath is drawn where a drain meets the river. Its limits are large: it speaks of junctions and side arms rather than field drains.
unsettled: British canal practice of about 1770-1850 straddles the Europe cut-off of about 1800.

why: It gives a third form of the samurai house's enclosure, a stone wall with a clipped hedge behind it. Chiran was one of Satsuma's rural samurai settlements rather than a castle town, so its form is regional. The page dates neither the walls nor the hedges. The defensive reason it gives for the hedge (seeing out without being seen) is visitor lore with nothing to back it, and we do not take it from here.
